name: Pasupatinathar Temple, Tirupanthanainallur
deity: Shiva as Pasupatinathar (Pasupatheeswarar), with the goddess Venubhujambikai (Veyurutholi Ammai)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of Chola Nadu, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); masonry temple from the Chola era (11th century) with later additions
dynasty: Chola (with later Chola and Vijayanagara patronage)
summary: Pasupatinathar is the Shiva temple of Pandanallur, the Tirupanthanainallur of the Tevaram, remembered for the tale of Parvati's game of ball, played with the four Vedas, and of the goddess who worshipped here in the form of a cow.

sections.history: Pandanallur lies in the Kaveri delta north of Aduthurai, in Thiruvidaimarudur taluk of Thanjavur district. In the Tevaram hymns of Sambandar and Appar it is Tirupanthanainallur, and the temple is counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams on the northern bank of the Kaveri. The oldest parts of the masonry temple that stands today belong to the Chola age, around the eleventh century. Inscriptions record gifts and works under later Chola kings, among them Vikrama Chola, Rajadhiraja II, Kulottunga III, and Rajaraja III, and there are gifts from the Vijayanagara period too. The shrine has been in unbroken worship from the days of the hymns to our own.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian complex of two enclosing prakaras, entered through a gopuram at the gateway. The sanctum holds Pasupatinathar as a linga, which tradition describes as self-manifested and white in colour, marked with the hoof of the cow and so not anointed in the usual way. The goddess Venubhujambikai is honoured in her own shrine. Within the temple is a sacred tank, the Surya Teertham, and the sacred tree is the sarakkonrai tree. Vinayaka is worshipped here as Nruthi Ganapathi, and the walls and corridors keep the inscriptions that tell the temple's long story.
sections.legends: The name of the place is the heart of its legend. Parvati wished to play at ball with her companions, and Shiva shaped balls for her from the four Vedas. She played on so long that the sun lingered in the sky and the sages could not close their evening rites. In the tradition, Parvati then took the form of a cow, with Murugan as her calf, and worshipped Shiva at this place until she was restored; Vishnu is said to have tended the cow as a herdsman. From this the lord is called Pasupatinathar, lord of the cattle, and the village is Pandanallur, the good place where the balls, the Vedas themselves, came to rest. Versions of the tale differ in its details, but all keep the cow, the ball, and the Vedas.
sections.festivals: Masi Magam in February or March and Panguni Uthiram in March or April are the great festivals of the temple. Maha Shivaratri, the Thirukarthigai lamps, and the Aippasi observances are kept with devotion, and the monthly Pradosham draws the faithful. One tradition holds that the sun worships the lord here by sending his rays upon the linga for three days in the month of Aavani. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Pandanallur is an unhurried visit. Enter beneath the gopuram, walk the prakaras reading the old inscriptions on the walls, and come to Pasupatinathar before turning to the goddess Venubhujambikai in her shrine. Take a moment at the Surya Teertham and at the shrine of Nruthi Ganapathi. The village is also known to lovers of dance, for it gave its name to the Pandanallur style of Bharatanatyam, shaped here by the teacher Meenakshisundaram Pillai, so the quiet streets around the temple carry a second kind of heritage. The cow-legend gives the visit a gentle, pastoral feeling that suits the green delta around it.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from the afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; listings differ, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Pandanallur is in the Kaveri delta, north of Aduthurai and between Kumbakonam and Mayiladuthurai, both of which have railway stations and frequent bus services onward to the village. Local buses and taxis reach the temple from either town. The nearest major airport is Tiruchirappalli, a few hours away by road.
